title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money, It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
dek: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants, and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
why: Medium information density, but the "time tax" framing itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about softening on UBI is worth hearing.
who: People working in public policy, govtech, or welfare products; engineers wondering whether AI can replace administrative processes; and readers who want to understand why the American welfare state is so inefficient.
skip: 36:25 to 38:28, the debate over how easy voting is — both sides talk past each other, low information gain.

points.h: The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
points.body: Lowrey's core example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries send you a pre-filled return and you just correct errors. The US could absolutely do this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, and their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This is not a technology problem, it's an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labor, and unlike a monetary tax, it's different: you can earn more money, you can't earn more time.

points.h: The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
points.body: Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) as the single worst program in government: nominally meant to address child poverty, it doesn't actually change the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely onerous and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are far better experiences, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. This yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of its beneficiaries.

points.h: Pandemic fraud isn't something the time tax can prevent
points.body: Cowen raises a common objection: after deregulation in 2020, fraud exploded, so maybe the time tax is a necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects this outright: the fraud came mainly from criminal gangs and fake small businesses, and from the fact that the UI system itself runs on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have zero incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so every recession replays the same conversation. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

points.h: Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
points.body: Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics, and hospital systems defrauding the government. Individual fraud has a low ceiling, because the amount you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud, you have to process a lot of paperwork. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organizations and legitimate providers, rather than burdening the 99.9% who don't commit fraud. She adds a political-economy note: fraud narratives are often used to make programs seem illegitimate, so voters tolerate cuts.

points.h: 50 hours per person per year, and highly unequal
points.body: Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She acknowledges this is an underestimate — ATUS can't capture multitasking (waiting on hold while cooking counts as one activity), and the time tax is scattered across categories without being aggregated. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip" it with subordinates and accountants, but there's one exception: renovating a house in San Francisco requires waiting 500 days and going through multiple rounds of public review no matter how rich you are.

points.h: AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
points.body: Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is unknown; second, many burdens aren't paperwork at all — they're mandatory interviews, urine screenings, hard-to-collect data. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, but the government has no stable definition of "household," and you have to explain how you split staple food costs with co-residents — a question AI would struggle to answer for you. She mentions she was originally skeptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years firmly believes AI will help a great deal.

points.h: Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
points.body: Cowen presses with data: from 1990 to 2014, the number of people on disability insurance roughly quadrupled while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the threshold be raised? Lowrey doesn't accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population aging and rising obesity-related chronic illness. Then she gives a counterpoint: 5% of applicants must submit over 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She admits she worries about both sides — both about paying people who don't need it and about denying people who truly do — so she doesn't think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

points.h: Her UBI stance has been shaken by the research
points.body: Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; this time she says explicitly that the research findings are "sobering," and she has updated her priors: the ancillary benefits she expected cash to deliver haven't materialized. But her defense is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improvements falling short of expectations is not a reason to oppose the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive back then of the claim that "AI will force UBI," and she won't go that far now, but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment also rises, that would be very strange, and we'd have to start considering UBI-type policies.

terms.def: The time cost imposed on individuals when government shifts administrative labor onto them; unlike a monetary tax, it cannot be offset by earning more money.
Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, the US cash welfare program; Lowrey considers it the most administratively burdensome and least effective program in government.
Benefits delivered through the tax code, where recipients often don't know they're receiving them, such as the child tax credit.
Efficiency gains lead to higher total consumption; Lowrey uses it to explain how labor-saving tools like email ultimately increased the volume of tasks.
Erroneous disbursements caused by complex rules, distinct from deliberate fraud; simplifying the rules can reduce them.

If you’re looking at what I think of as roughly as bureaucratic time total spent, it’s 50 hours per person per year.

I’m convinced that white-collar technology, labor-saving stuff, I’m convinced it’s all Jevons paradoxical. I think that basically anything that is designed like email to make your life easier will at some point make it worse.
